TRANSCRIPT:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we'll kick off  i'm jordan from redwood, i run the ae for this account. priya is our se, she'll lead the demo and the deep dive bits.
[00:08] Carlos: thanks jordan, appreciate it. we got a couple goals, short version: we need to understand if redwood can handle our real-time summarization pipeline  long conversation history (up to 200k tokens), and bursts up to ~8k TPS, sometimes sustained.
[00:18] Priya: awesome, thanks carlos. quick clarification  when you say 200k tokens do you mean full context is stored and fed as one request, or you expect incremental KV cache usage?
[00:25] Asha: sorry, yes full context for the first pass  user session history is pre-appended for the top-level summarizer, but we can stream incremental updates too.
[00:33] Priya: got it. we'll demo two modes: 1) long-context path (prefix caching + retrieve-and-compile) and 2) high TPS path with streaming where we show backpressure / timeout handling. note  some transcribed words may be off in this export, "KV cash" shows up sometimes in our notes, that's just transcription.
[00:45] Maya: quick note  we'll reference the Optimize console recommendations and the autoscaling policy we recommend for sustained >5k TPS.
[00:50] Liam: also we have strict VPC peering rules and can't open public endpoints for the pilot unless we go through their private deployment option. security is a must.
[00:57] Jordan: understood, we'll cover private deployment options and KMS/SSO briefly. ok priya, demo?

[05:12] Priya: launching screen share  Redwood Console -> Model Catalog. so first, long-context path: our runtime supports prefix/KV cache and chunked attention patterns. for your 200k token artifact, we recommend storing session prefixes in the kv cache and only materializing recent tokens to reduce token-cost and memory pressure. graph here is our heuristic, but main point is: caching avoids re-encoding long prefixes on every request.
[05:37] Asha: are you recomputing the kv cache per user, or do you reuse across similar sessions?
[05:41] Priya: per user sessions, yes, keys are session-scoped. you can set a TTL and eviction policy in the Console. note  the console UI label sometimes says "KV cash" in older builds, we've filed a ticket.
[06:00] Carlos: what's the memory footprint per session if we keep a 200k-token cache?
[06:04] Priya: rough ballpark: depends on quantization and model block size. with 8-bit quantization and our optimized KV layout you should expect xGB per 100k tokens on an A100-class instance; we'll produce precise numbers in the benchmark.
[06:22] Priya: next, high TPS demo  switching to the API tab. we'll simulate 6k TPS sustained with concurrent connections and show our batching + routing logic. note we typically recommend Dedicated capacity for predictable throughput at that scale.
[06:38] Jordan: just to call it out  Hosted can do burst, but dedicated GPU pools reduce queuing jitter and give you an SLA.

[12:10] Priya: starting streaming test now. this is a simulated client that open streams and continuously sends prompt windows. watch the server side metrics: inflight tokens, queue depth, and backpressure events.
[12:22] (sound of keyboard, screen share showing dashboard)
[12:30] Priya: ok at 4k TPS we see median latency ~120ms token, 95th ~280ms. as we ramp to 8k the runtime triggers batching windows and queue depth increases; you'll see some streaming backpressure events flagged.
[12:45] Asha: what exactly happens on the client when backpressure triggers? do we drop connections or do we get partial chunks?
[12:51] Priya: good q  we surface backpressure as a 429-streaming event on the websocket and the client SDK will attempt exponential reconnect with resume token. note there are two failure modes we've seen: 1) client timeouts before reconnect completes (leading to partial outputs), 2) server-side stream timeouts (if a token generation path stalls). we recommend a combination of client-side buffering, resume tokens, and idempotent request ids.
[13:18] Carlos: can you demo a timeout case?
[13:22] Priya: yeah  i'll force a delayed kernel selection to simulate a stall. (demo) stream emits a partial chunk then sends a stream-timeout event, the client SDK retries with the same request-id and retrieves the remainder from our cache/fallback route. sometimes transcription will show provider names wrong  e.g., "Big Cloud" in the logs is our internal sim.
[14:00] Liam: if the client retries quickly won't that amplify the load and make the queue worse?
[14:04] Priya: exactly  that's where our circuit-breaker + adaptive backoff policy helps. we throttle retries at the SDK layer and optionally route retries to a cheaper model variant to avoid amplifying load.

[18:20] Jordan: circling back to security  will SOC2 and KMS integration be available for Dedicated and Private?
[18:26] Maya: yes  we support customer-managed KMS in Dedicated and Private deployments, SOC 2 Type II report available, SAML/SSO and RBAC for console. we'll attach the security pack in the follow up.
[18:40] Nora: any compliance issues with long-context caching (we keep PII in session history)?
[18:46] Priya: you can encrypt session-level KV entries with your KMS keys and set retention/auto-purge policies; for air-gapped private deployments we can isolate storage entirely in your VPC.

[22:55] Priya: quick note about cost: long context without caching is expensive  3-5x token cost increase we typically see. Optimize console gives quantization + batching recommendations; for your workload we expect a 2.5-3x cost reduction by combining 8-bit quant + prefix caching.
[23:12] Carlos: do you have any benchmark numbers for 8k TPS sustained with long context?
[23:18] Priya: we have internal runs that show 8k TPS with 100ms token latency on optimized configs using dedicated pools and custom kernels, but your actual numbers depend on model size, sequence lengths, and quantization. we'll run a customer-specific 24-72 hour benchmark.

[30:05] Priya: now, streaming backpressure handling detail  here are the key levers: adaptive batching window, per-tenant queue limits, retry routing to model variants, and client-side resume tokens. in the console you can configure these as part of the route.
[30:27] Asha: how granular is the autoscaler? will it spin up GPUs instantly on a sudden 2x spike?
[30:32] Priya: autoscaling has cooldowns; for instant bursts we recommend reserved burst capacity attached to Dedicated pools. bursting spins up within ~90-120 seconds typically. for sub-second bursts we rely on queued tokens + cheaper model route.

[36:40] Jordan: procurement question  what does a pilot look like? can we do a private deployment pilot with limited nodes?
[36:47] Maya: yes, pilot can be private control plane + a small on-prem/dedicated pool. we'll provide template MSA, SOC2, and an addendum for private deployment.
[36:55] Carlos: costs for a pilot?
[36:58] Jordan: we'll share the pricing spreadsheet  usually a 4-6 week pilot with a small committed pool. specifics in the follow up.

[42:12] Priya: closing notes: two technical risks to flag  1) if you attempt to naively replay 200k token contexts on every request you'll hit memory and cost ceilings; 2) naive client retry behavior can amplify backpressure. both are solvable with KV/prefix caching and circuit-breakers.
[42:32] Nora: ok that helps. can you include sample SDK patterns for resume tokens and idempotency?
[42:36] Priya: yes will attach code snippets and an sdk best-practices doc link in the follow-up.
